claims.text: Spin-polarized density functional theory can be used to detect and characterize ferromagnetic ground states in transition-metal alloys.
Spin-polarized DFT explicitly includes spin polarization and exchange interactions in electronic-structure calculations.
A spin-polarized configuration having lower total energy than a nonmagnetic configuration indicates a ferromagnetic ground state.
Partially filled d orbitals in a transition-metal alloy may support local magnetic moments.
Exchange splitting in transition-metal d orbitals is captured in the computed electronic density.
Comparing the total energies of different magnetic configurations determines the energetic favorability of spin alignment.
Favorable exchange interactions can lower the energy of a ferromagnetically aligned state.
A ferromagnetic ground state should produce a lower calculated energy for the ferromagnetic configuration and nonzero atomic magnetic moments.
Non-spin-polarized DFT does not represent exchange splitting or the associated stabilization of magnetic ordering.
The predicted magnetic state and its quantitative properties depend on the selected exchange-correlation functional.
Standard DFT may be limited by its treatment of electron correlation.
Static 0 K DFT calculations do not capture finite-temperature effects and dynamical fluctuations.
Spin-polarized DFT can reliably indicate a tendency toward ferromagnetic ordering.
Calculated energy differences and magnetic moments may require experimental verification by SQUID magnetometry.
Substrate effects or strong electron correlations can cause quantitative uncertainty in the predicted magnetic properties.

contradictions.description: The conditions appropriately distinguish ferromagnetic, nonmagnetic, and antiferromagnetic configurations, but the mechanism groups antiferromagnetic states with non-spin-polarized states. An antiferromagnetic calculation is normally spin-polarized despite having zero or small net magnetization.

The hypothesis states that lower energy relative to only a nonmagnetic state establishes a ferromagnetic ground state, whereas the conditions call for comparison with antiferromagnetic configurations. A ferromagnetic state below the nonmagnetic state is not necessarily the ground state if an antiferromagnetic or other magnetic configuration is still lower.
